row.story:
Leni found Mrs Bell winding a red-and-white spool beside the village hall. “Could I borrow it for the welcome bunting? I’ll bring back the leftover string.” Mrs Bell passed it over. “The spool, please—not the bunting.” Leni looked toward the bare square posts. They seemed to be waiting for a party.

Jo, the new neighbor, sat on the square bench with a walking boot beside them. “I wanted to help with the festival,” Jo said, “but I’m not climbing anything until this ankle heals.” Leni started to offer to do it alone, then stopped. “Would you help me choose where it goes?” Jo smiled. “Now that’s a proper invitation.”

Leni and Jo looked from the arch to the low posts. The square was calm and dry; both posts held firm, the spool reached far enough, and Jo could reach the line. “No climbing,” Jo said. “We can both reach this.” Leni chose a line fifty-five centimetres high. The arch stayed bare, but the square had a plan for both of them.

Leni clipped the red and white triangles along the square posts, keeping the line at 55 centimetres. Jo tied the final knot from the bench, without climbing or stretching for the arch. Their knot held on the first careful tug. The borrowed string now had a job: holding the welcome where both neighbors could reach it.

Mrs Bell opened the doors at the square, and the first neighbors followed the red-and-white bunting to the tables. “We had a grander plan,” Leni said, “but this is the one we made together.” Jo pointed out a favorite triangle and told its story. People gathered to listen; the welcome had become something Jo could give, too.

After the first rush of the festival, Leni carried Mrs Bell’s spool back to the hall cupboard, with the unused string wound neatly around it. The used length still held the bunting in place. “You put it to work,” Mrs Bell said. Jo was showing a neighbor the knot. Leni was glad to return the spool with something useful left on it.

The square filled beneath the low line, and nobody needed a ladder or a rescue. Jo showed two children how to tie the same secure knot, while Leni welcomed the late arrivals. The arch remained empty; the square did not. By the time the music started, Jo was laughing with people who had come to meet their new neighbor.
